description: The goal of this course is to prepare graduate students to perform scientific data analysis using the R programming language.  Successful students will learn how to use statistical inference and machine-learning tools to gain insight into data sets, as well as be introduced to techniques and best practises for storing, managing and analyzing data.  Topics will include: R programming, version control, modular programming, coding best practices, data analysis, machine learning and scientific visualization.Students willing to take the course as part of their graduate program must enrol through Acorn.  This course is part of the IMS graduate program.
title: MSC1090 - Lecture 11

description:
With recent updates to privacy legislation across multiple provinces in Canada, personal information protection in research settings is often confusing and challenging for both researchers and research administration. This webinar will highlight the complexities in applying current Quebec privacy legislation in research contexts and explore the structural and administrative support required in this process.  The presenters will examine the roles of researchers and research administration support, exploring both tensions and opportunities to operationalize “Privacy by Design” in research settings.

**About the Speakers**
Marie-Christine Boulianne: After working for several years as a clinical research coordinator, Marie-Christine is now a research ethics advisor at a large health and social services institution in Montreal. Her work focuses primarily on research ethics, data governance, and the protection of personal information. She works on issues related to access to, use, and sharing of research data, as well as the application of Quebec’s Laws 5 & 25 in health research. Her particular interest lies in finding the right balance between data access, privacy protection, and security requirements. 

Biru Zhou is the Senior Advisor for Research Data Management in the Office of VP (Research and Innovation) at McGill University, a role she has held since 2021. Her work focuses on reshaping research data management (RDM) services toward collaborative, multi-stakeholder models. She co-authored the article "There's no 'I' in Research Data Management: Reshaping RDM Services Toward a Collaborative Multi-Stakeholder Model," as well as several book chapters on the Canadian and international RDM landscape. She is passionate about promoting best RDM practices in research.

description:
Artificial intelligence is transforming the enterprise, academic and research landscapes, from accelerating discovery and data analysis to reshaping teaching, publishing, and scholarly communication. While these technologies offer unprecedented opportunities for innovation, they also raise critical questions about research integrity, bias, transparency, accountability, and the responsible use of data.
This AI Fireside Chat brings together experts in AI research, ethics, cybersecurity, and privacy to examine the challenges and opportunities associated with AI adoption in higher education and research environments. Panelists will discuss emerging concerns including the use of generative AI, protection of high and very high-risk research data, ethical considerations with AI use and development in research, and the growing need for governance frameworks that foster both innovation and trust. Attendees will gain practical insights into how institutions and researchers can leverage AI responsibly while maintaining the rigor, integrity, and credibility that underpin academic scholarship. 

**About the Panelists**

**Taylor Bohn** is a Senior Privacy and Information Security Risk Advisor at the University of British Columbia (UBC), where he advises academic and administrative units on privacy, cybersecurity, AI governance, and cloud service adoption. His work focuses on helping project teams make informed decisions about emerging technologies by assessing privacy, security, and operational risks. Taylor has led privacy and security reviews for a wide range of services and enterprise platforms. 

**Sarah Flann** serves as Research Ethics Review Officer for the University of British Columbia's (UBC) Behavioural Research Ethics Board, where she supports the ethical review and oversight of research involving human participants. Throughout her career, she has worked with several research ethics boards (REB), including UBC's Clinical REB, the Fraser Health REB, and Adler University Vancouver's REB.

Prior to transitioning into research ethics, Sarah spent a decade managing complex research studies in clinical neuroscience, psychosis, and neuroimaging. She holds a Master of Science in Psychology and Neuroscience of Mental Health from King's College London and has contributed to the development of ethical guidance for patient-oriented research. She has a particular interest in the ethical implications of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, and their impact on research integrity, transparency, accountability, and public trust in academic research.

**Vered Shwartz** is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at the University of British Columbia, a CIFAR AI Chair at the Vector Institute, and the author of "Lost in Automatic Translation: Navigating Life in English in the Age of Language Technologies". Her current research focus is on (1) testing and improving the capabilities of large language models and vision and language models; (2) developing culturally-competent AI; and (3) responsible NLP applications in sensitive domains (e.g., legal, medical). Before joining UBC, she was a postdoctoral researcher at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) and the University of Washington. Prior to that, she completed her PhD in Computer Science at Bar-Ilan University.

**Scott Baker** manages both the Research Cybersecurity and Compliance team at UBC Advanced Research Computing and the Compliance Support Team at UBC. Both groups are focused on supporting researchers and staff in navigating compliance requirements and finding secure solutions for their project architectures and data. He is a member of the program leadership committee for UBC's Privacy & Information Security Management program.
organizer: National Security Council (NSC) - Security Training and Awareness Group
title: AI Fireside Chat: Responsible Use of AI in Academia: Opportunities, Risks, and Research Integrity

Abstract: Autonomous AI will make the coming few years interesting when it comes to cybersecurity ... whether we are talking about malicious bots unleashed on the web or about your own agents roaming your system!  
It is time to think about hardening your machine and adopting better practices.  
In this webinar, I will:
- go over basic safety rules,
- explain key concepts of filesystem permissions, secure shells (key pairs, SSH agents), and public key cryptography (key structure, OpenPGP, GPG agents),
- and finally demo several open source tools for data encryption and password management (e.g. Sequoia-PGP, KeePassXC, gocryptfs).
title: Hardening your system in the age of AI [webinar]

description:
Let us be your body double with this in-person bootcamp! Data Management Plans (DMPs) are both incredibly helpful research tools and increasingly required for grants but it can hard to know how to complete a Data Management Plan if it’s your first time. **This session is carefully timed for researchers completing a CFI or Tri-Agency grant this fall.** If you're in the process of creating a DMP, either for a grant application or for your own research, join RDM Services for this afternoon session. The RDM services team will provide tailored guidance as you write your plan on site, and we'll have some light snacks and refreshments to keep you going. Come away with a clear path forward or even a finished DMP!

This participatory session is especially relevant for researchers at all levels in the beginning stages of a research project or streamlining best practices for their research team. Come on your own, send your research staff, or bring your whole research group. Let us know if you're joining as a research team - we'll make sure you get a table to work together at!

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

1. Identify the 5 key components of a data management plan (DMP).
2. Compare strong and weak responses in each section of a DMP.
3. Develop a tailored outline, or potentially a complete draft, of their own DMP!

**Details:** Any preparatory work for the session can be found on its [information page](https://learn.scds.ca/rdm26-27/dmp-oct.html). This virtual workshop will be recorded and shared on the same page, and discoverable via the Sherman Centre's [Online Learning Catalogue.](https://scds.ca/searchable-online-learning/)

**Certificate Eligibility:** This workshop is eligible for the Sherman Centre's certificate program. For more information, visit [scds.ca/certificate-program](http://scds.ca/certificate-program). It is also eligible for the Canadian Certificate for Digital Humanities. To learn more, visit [ccdhhn.ca](http://ccdhhn.ca/) or contact [scds@mcmaster.ca](mailto:scds@mcmaster.ca).

description:
Learn the basics of using Git and GitHub for version control and collaboration. Git is widely used version control software that tracks changes to a group of files, referred to as a repository. GitHub is a popular website for hosting and sharing Git repositories, making it easier to collaborate and share your work. Together, Git and GitHub provide a platform that is increasingly used for collaboration in research and academic environments. In this beginner workshop participants will learn key concepts, create their own Git repository, and publish to GitHub. No previous experience with Git is required. Familiarity with the command line interface will be helpful but is not necessary. This is part 1 of a two-part introductory workshop.

**Pre-workshop setup**

Please complete the [pre-workshop setup](https://ubc-library-rc.github.io/intro-git/) to install the Bash shell and Git. If you don't already have one, create a free GitHub account before the workshop. 

This workshop is part of the [Core Skills](https://libcal.library.ubc.ca/calendar/vancouver/?t=g&q=Core%20Skills&cid=7544&cal=7544&inc=0)series.

description: Thanks to ACENET’s generosity, we have subsidized the registration costs for this workshop. This 3-day workshop offers a beginner-friendly hands-on introduction to machine learning and its application to bioinformatics. This workshop is not intended for machine learning experts; instead, it targets biologists or other life scientists who want to understand what machine learning is, what it can do and how it can be used for a variety of bioinformatic applications.
prerequisites: Familiar with the basics of Python. You will also require your own laptop computer. Minimum requirements: 1024×768 screen resolution, 1.5GHz CPU, 2GB RAM, 10GB free disk space, recent versions of Windows, Mac OS X or Linux (Most computers purchased in the past 3-4 years likely meet these requirements). If you do not have access to your own computer, you may loan one from the CBW. Please contact support@bioinformatics.ca for more information. This workshop requires participants to complete pre-workshop tasks and readings.
title: (2026) Machine Learning Foundations: Halifax, NS

Machine learning and AI technologies are transforming science, but knowing how to get started can feel overwhelming. This intensive 3-day hands-on workshop offered by the Canadian Bioinformatics Workshops through bioinformatics.ca introduces foundational concepts and methods of machine learning with practical examples and exercises.
You will gain experience in:

• Applications and limitations of machine learning and deep learning;

• Decision trees and random forests;

• Artificial neural networks (ANNs);

• Fundamentals of clustering as an unsupervised machine learning method;

• Machine learning operations principles; and

• Applying these machine learning techniques for biomarker discovery, secondary structure prediction and more.
CBW have been teaching bioinformatics for over 25 years, reaching over 4000 students through more than 200 workshops. Learn from our experts, network with peers, and start your Machine Learning journey!
Only 30 seats are available, so reserve your seat today!
